Loading packages and data:

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
```


# Problem 1
The NY NOAA dataset is compiled from the NOAA NCEI daily database of summary stats from weather stations in the world. This data is focused on the NY state weather stations. 

The key variables are: 

* id: weather station ID
* date: date of observation
* prcp: precipitation (in tenths of mm)
* snow: snowfall (mm)
* snwd: snow depth (mm)
* tmax: maximum temperature (tenths of degrees C)
* tmin: minimum temperature (tenths of degrees C)

There is extensive missing data. 
```{r}
ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~ mean(is.na(.)) * 100
    )
  )
```
We see that prcp has 5.6% missing, snow has 14.7% missing, snwd has 22.8% missing, tmax has 43.7% missing, and tmin has 43.7% missing

## We will clean the data
Generate seperate variables for month date and year. In addition convert prcp, tmax, tmin to units of mm and degrees C respectively. 
```{r}
ny_noaa_df = 
  ny_noaa |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    date = ymd(date),
    day = day(date),
    month = month(date),
    year = year(date)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    prcp = prcp / 10,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  )
```

## Most common snow fall recorded

```{r}
ny_noaa_df |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE)
```

The most commonly recorded snow fall is 0 mm at 2008508. 

## Displaying the average max temperature in January and July in each station across years

```{r fig.width=14}
jan_ny_noaa_df =
  ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(month == 1) |>
  group_by(id, year) |>
  summarize(
    jan_tmax_average = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = jan_tmax_average, group = id)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(
    title = "January",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average daily maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

july_ny_noaa_df =
  ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(month == 7) |>
  group_by(id, year) |>
  summarize(
    july_tmax_average = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = july_tmax_average, group = id)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(
    title = "July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average daily maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
  
jan_ny_noaa_df + july_ny_noaa_df + plot_annotation(
    title = "Average Daily Maximum Temperature by Station and Year"
  )

```

In January, average max temperatures at each station on a yearly basis tend to correlate with one another. For example, in 1990, temperatures are generally all higher compared to in 2010 or 2009. It also seems that the temperatures are overall increasing in January from 1981 to 1990. The year to year variation seems less in July compared to Janauary. In addition, July temperatures are overall higher than January, as expected. There does seem to be outliers in the data as evidenced by weather station points that are distant from the average for each month. For example, in January 2005, there appears to be one station that has a much lower average maximum temperature than the rest. 

## Comparing T max and Tmin and Snowfall Values

We will create a violin plot for T max and Tmin and snow fall excluding less than 0 mm and greater or equal to 100 mm 
```{r fig.width=14}

temperature_boxplot = 
  ny_noaa_df |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = "tmax", y = tmax), na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = "tmin", y = tmin), na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "All Maximum and Minimum Temperatures",
    x = "Temperature type",
    y = "Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

snowfall_boxplot = 
  ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of snowfall by year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

temperature_boxplot + snowfall_boxplot + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 2))
```

As expected, Tmax on average is higher than Tmin with a wider IQR. There are outliers in both Tmin and Tmax as seen by the dots on the boxpllots. 

For snowfall, the average snowfall appears to consistently be 25 mm with outliers in 1998 2006 and 2010. This is in context of limiting our data to only display snowfall from 0 to < 100 mm. 

# Problem 2

## Data importa and tidying
We merge the NHANES covars and accel data followed by excluding subjects < 21 years of age and anyone with missing demographic data. We convert sex and education to factor variables with relevant labeling which is more appropriate.
```{r}
nhanes_covar =
  read.csv("./data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes_accel = 
  read.csv("./data/nhanes_accel.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes_df = 
  nhanes_covar |>
  left_join(nhanes_accel, by = "seqn") |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  mutate(
    sex = 
      case_match(
        sex, 
        1 ~ "male", 
        2 ~ "female"),
    sex = as.factor(sex), 
    education = 
      case_match (
        education,
        1 ~ "Less than high school",
        2 ~ "High school equivalent",
        3 ~ "More than high school"),
    education = as.factor(education)
  )
```

## Men and Women in Each Education Group

Here we display the amount of men in each education category and women in each education category
```{r}
nhanes_df |>
  group_by(sex, education) |> 
  summarize(count = n())
  
```
We see that a majority of females and males had more than a high school education. 

Now we display the age distributions of females and males with varying educational levels. 
```{r}
nhanes_df |>
  select(education, sex, age) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_grid(~ education) +
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis(discrete = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Age distributions by sex and education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
We see that older females more frequently completed high school equivalent compared to older males. 
In addition, we see that younger females more frequently completed more than high school than younger females. The less than high school category is roughly similar. 

## Plotting the total daily activity per individuals and educational group

We want to determine the daily activity total by age, sex, and education level.

First we create a new data frame with a total activity variable.Then, plot each total activity level vs age in each education group. 
```{r}
nhanes_df_total_activity = 
  nhanes_df |>
  mutate(
    total_activity = rowSums(pick(starts_with("min")))
  )
nhanes_df_total_activity |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily activity total by age, sex, and education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total daily activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

```
We've displayed three plots. We see that in those with high school equivalent education, younger females seemed to be more active than younger males. As age increased, the two trends seem to converge and activity decreaes. In those who completed less than high school and more than high school educations, females and male activity decreased with increasing age. 

## Plotting the trend in activity per each individual and educational group

Now we will plot the trend in daily activity level per sex and educational group.Given the amount of datapoints, we will hide the individual datapoints and only display the fitted curve to understand the general trends. 

```{r fig.width= 14}
nhanes_df_24h_acitivty =
  nhanes_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "activity"
  )|>
  mutate(
    minute = readr::parse_number(minute)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "24-hr activity trend by sex, and education",
    x = "Minute",
    y = "MIMS",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

nhanes_df_24h_acitivty
```

We see that across all educational groups and both sexes, activity is low from 000 and rises around 0800h. Activity the decreases in the evening time. This is expected. 

# Problem 3

## Import and Clean Data

First we import and clean the data. 

```{r}
jan_2020_citi = 
  read.csv("./data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(date = "2020-01")

jan_2024_citi = 
  read.csv("./data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(date = "2024-01")

july_2020_citi = 
  read.csv("./data/July 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(date = "2020-07")

july_2024_citi = 
  read.csv("./data/July 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(date = "2024-07")

citi_df = 
  bind_rows(jan_2020_citi, july_2020_citi, jan_2024_citi, july_2024_citi) |>
  mutate(
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type),
    member_casual = factor(member_casual),
    date = factor(date),
    weekdays = factor(weekdays, levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
        "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
    )
  )) |>
  relocate(ride_id, date, weekdays)
```
We've now binded the ride information from all of the months. We created a tibble with a new variable date that represents what year and month of the ride. We converted rideable_type to a factor variable representing classic or electric rides. Weekdays converted to factor as well. Also, member_casual is now a factor variable representing member or casual status. Reordered the variables so that date and weekday are adjacent to ride_id. 

Key variables: 
* ride_id: ride ID
* date: year and month of ride
* weekdays: day of week of ride
* duration: duration of ride in minutes
* rideable_type: electric or classic bike
* member_casual: citi bike member or casual 
* start_station_name and end_station_name: start and end station name respecitvely. 

Number of unique rides: `r citi_df |> summarize(n_distinct(ride_id))`

Mean ride duration: `r citi_df |> summarize(mean(duration))` minutes

## Reader Friendly Table Showing Total Numbers of Rides by Date and Separating Rider Type

Now we create a table that shows the total number of rides by Date and Rider Type
```{r}
citi_df |>
  group_by(date, member_casual) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_rides = n_distinct(ride_id, na.rm = TRUE)
  )|>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = number_of_rides
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Number of Rides by Date and Rider Type"
  )
```

Here we see that there were more member rides than casual rides in all months included. Also, there is increasing casual and member rides overall with time. 

## The five most common starting points for rides:
```{r}
citi_df |>
  group_by(start_station_name) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_rides = n_distinct(ride_id, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(number_of_rides)) |>
  head(5) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Five most popular starting stations"
  )
```

We see that W 21 st & 6 Ave is the most popular location. 

## Understanding the effect of weekdays, month, and year on median ride duration

We will now generate a plot displaying the effect of weekday on median ride durtion and the effect of date: 
```{r fig.width = 14, fig.height = 6}
weekday_median_duration =   
  citi_df |>
  group_by(weekdays) |>
  summarize(median_duration = median(duration)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration)) +
  geom_point(aes(weekdays), alpha = .5) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(
    x = "Weekday", 
    y = "Median Ride Duration (Minutes)",
    ) 

month_median_duration = 
  citi_df |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarize(median_duration = median(duration)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(date), y = median_duration)) +
  geom_point(aes(date), alpha = .5) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(
    x = "Date", 
    y = "Median Ride Duration (Minutes)",
    ) 

weekday_median_duration + month_median_duration + plot_annotation(
    title = "Citi Bike Median Ride Duration by Weekday and Date")
```

Here we see taht median ride durations were higher on Saturday and Sunday.
We also see that median ride duration increased between in July compared to January. In addiiton, there seems to be lower overall rides in July 2024 compared to July 2020. This may be due to the COVID19 pandemic increasing median ride duration in July 2020.  

## Understanding the association of bike type with ride duration

```{r}
citi_df |>
  filter(date %in% c("2024-01", "2024-07")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(date), y = duration, fill = member_casual)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ rideable_type) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration by Month, Membership, and Bike Type in 2024",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Ride duration (minutes)",
    fill = "Membership status"
  )
```
Here we see that Electric Bikes had an apparent longer median duration in casual riders vs. members in both January and July of 2024. Among members, electric bikes appeared to have longer median ride duration in July 2024 vs. January 2024. In classic bikes, the median duration among members appeared similar in July vs. January 2024.
